s.line: When Dorothy was left alone she began to feel hungry.
s.note: נִשְׁאַר is nif'al with an active meaning, "to remain, stay", so English "was left" comes out as an ordinary active verb in Hebrew. רְעֵבָה is the feminine of רָעֵב (hungry); the adjective agrees with Dorothy. In speech you'll hear אֲנִי מֵת מֵרָעָב (I'm starving, lit. dying of hunger).

s.line: So she went to the cupboard and cut herself some bread, which she spread with butter.
s.note: מָרַח = to spread (butter, jam, cream). The noun מִמְרָח is any spread, such as מִמְרַח שׁוֹקוֹלָד. Note how the Hebrew turns "which she spread with butter" around: she spread butter on it, עָלָיו.

s.line: She gave some to Toto,
and taking a pail from the shelf she carried it down to the little brook and filled it with clear, sparkling water.
s.note: מִלֵּא (pi'el) = to fill, from the same root as מָלֵא (full). It takes a direct object and then בְּ: מִלְּאָה אוֹתוֹ בְּמַיִם. You also מְמַלְּאִים טֹפֶס (fill in a form). מַיִם is always plural, so its adjectives are plural too: מַיִם צְלוּלִים.

s.line: Toto ran over to the trees and began to bark at the birds sitting there.
s.note: A dog barks עַל someone: נָבַח עַל. The same preposition goes with shouting at someone, צָעַק עַל, and figuratively הוּא נוֹבֵחַ עַל כֻּלָּם (he snaps at everyone).

s.line: Dorothy went to get him,
and saw such delicious fruit hanging from the branches that she gathered some of it,
s.note: תָּלוּי is a pa'ul (passive) participle of תָּלָה (to hang something up): "hung", hence "hanging". It also means "depends": זֶה תָּלוּי בְּךָ = it's up to you. כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ = "so … that". קָטַף is the verb for picking fruit or flowers.

s.line: finding it just what she wanted to help out her breakfast.
s.note: הִשְׁלִים (hif'il) = to complete, to fill in what is missing. Related: שָׁלֵם (whole), and the everyday הַשְׁלָמָה (make-up session, e.g. שִׁעוּר הַשְׁלָמָה). פֵּרוֹת is masculine plural, so here it is הֵם.

s.line: Then she went back to the house,
s.note: הַבַּיְתָה = "homeward". The ending ָה shows direction, as in צָפוֹנָה (northward) and יָמִינָה (to the right). הַבַּיְתָה is still everyday speech: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ הַבַּיְתָה.

s.line: and having helped herself and Toto to a good drink of the cool, clear water,
s.note: לָרְוָיָה = "to satisfaction, one's fill", said of drinking and, figuratively, of anything: נָשַׁמְנוּ אֲוִיר צַח לָרְוָיָה. קָרִיר = cool, pleasantly chilly, milder than קַר (cold).

s.line: she set about making ready for the journey to the City of Emeralds.
s.note: הִתְכּוֹנֵן (hitpa'el) = to prepare oneself, take לְ: לְהִתְכּוֹנֵן לְמִבְחָן (to prepare for a test). Its pi'el sibling כִּוֵּן means to aim or adjust, and הִתְכַּוֵּן means to mean or intend.

s.line: Dorothy had only one other dress,
but that happened to be clean and was hanging on a peg beside her bed.
s.note: בְּמִקְרֶה = "by chance", the natural way to say "happened to": בְּמִקְרֶה רָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ (I happened to see him). As a question it is the polite "by any chance?": יֵשׁ לְךָ בְּמִקְרֶה עֵט? The dress is הִיא because שִׂמְלָה is feminine.

s.line: It was gingham, with checks of white and blue;
s.note: מְשֻׁבָּץ (pu'al participle) = checked, in squares. The noun מִשְׁבֶּצֶת is a square on a board or a slot in a schedule, and the pi'el שִׁבֵּץ means to slot someone in or assign: שִׁבְּצוּ אוֹתִי לַמִּשְׁמֶרֶת (they put me on the shift). Gingham is a checked cotton cloth.

s.line: and although the blue was somewhat faded with many washings, it was still a pretty frock.
s.note: לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ = although, the everyday choice; אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ means the same but is more formal. דָּהָה = to fade (colors); דָּהוּי = faded, as in גִּ׳ינְס דָּהוּי. כְּבִיסָה = washing, and also "the laundry": לִתְלוֹת כְּבִיסָה.

s.line: The girl washed herself carefully, dressed herself in the clean gingham, and tied her pink sunbonnet on her head.
s.note: הִתְרַחֵץ is hitpa'el, the reflexive binyan: רָחַץ = to wash (something), הִתְרַחֵץ = to wash oneself. Compare הִתְלַבֵּשׁ (to get dressed). With a named garment, though, Hebrew uses pa'al לָבַשׁ + object: לָבְשָׁה אֶת הַשִּׂמְלָה.

s.line: She took a little basket and filled it with bread from the cupboard, laying a white cloth over the top.
s.note: פָּרַשׂ = to spread out (a cloth, a map, wings). Don't confuse it with פָּרַשׁ (with שׁ), "to retire, withdraw": הוּא פָּרַשׁ מֵהַפּוֹלִיטִיקָה. Without niqqud the two look the same: פרש.

s.line: Then she looked down at her feet and noticed how old and worn her shoes were.
s.note: שָׂם לֵב ("put heart") = to notice, pay attention; with לְ for the thing: שִׂים לֵב לַמַּדְרֵגָה! (mind the step!). In reported thought Hebrew keeps the present tense: "noticed how old they are". בָּלוּי = worn out, a pa'ul participle of בָּלָה (to wear out).

s.line: “They surely will never do for a long journey, Toto,” she said.
s.note: הִתְאִים (hif'il) = to suit, be right for, with לְ: זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי (this doesn't suit me / doesn't work for me), a phrase you'll hear daily. The adjective is מַתְאִים (suitable). בֶּטַח = surely, probably; alone it means "sure!".

w: הֵרִים מַבָּט|looked up|~lit. raised a look
s.line: And Toto looked up into her face with his little black eyes and wagged his tail to show he knew what she meant.
s.note: כִּשְׁכֵּשׁ בַּזָּנָב = to wag the tail, with בְּ: you wag with the tail. It is a four-letter root built by doubling, like נִדְנֵד (to swing). לְמָה הִיא מִתְכַּוֶּנֶת = "what she means"; לְמָה אַתָּה מִתְכַּוֵּן? = "what do you mean?".

s.line: At that moment Dorothy saw lying on the table the silver shoes that had belonged to the Witch of the East.
s.note: מֻנָּח is a hof'al participle, the passive of הֵנִיחַ (to put down): "placed", so "lying" for objects. הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת מֻנָּחִים עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן = the keys are on the table. Note the word order רָאֲתָה דּוֹרוֹתִי: after a time phrase, written Hebrew often puts the verb first.

s.line: “I wonder if they will fit me,” she said to Toto.
s.note: מְעַנְיֵן אִם ("it's interesting if") is how Hebrew says "I wonder if / whether": מְעַנְיֵן אִם הוּא יָבוֹא. מְעַנְיֵן מָה … = I wonder what … . The same הִתְאִים לְ from sentence 19 now means "fit" (in size).

w: מָה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ|what is needed|~idiom: just the thing
s.line: “They would be just the thing to take a long walk in, for they could not wear out.”
s.note: נִשְׁחַק (nif'al) = to wear down, wear out; שָׁחוּק = worn. Without niqqud it is spelled just like שָׂחַק (with שׂ), "to play", and a worn-out word or idea is שָׁחוּק: בְּדִיחָה שְׁחוּקָה (a stale joke).

s.line: She took off her old leather shoes and tried on the silver ones,
s.note: מָדַד = to measure, and also to try on clothes: אֶפְשָׁר לִמְדֹּד? (can I try it on?) is what you ask in a shop, and the fitting room is תָּא מְדִידָה. הוֹרִיד (hif'il of יָרַד, "to make go down") is the everyday verb for taking off shoes or clothes.

s.line: which fitted her as well as if they had been made for her.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al) here is the passive of עָשָׂה: "was made". It also means "became" (נַעֲשָׂה קַר, it got cold) and "was going on": מָה נַעֲשֶׂה? = what's happening?, and also "what shall we do?". כְּאִלּוּ = as if; in slang it is a filler, like English "like".

s.line: Finally she picked up her basket.
“Come along, Toto,” she said.
“We will go to the Emerald City and ask the Great Oz how to get back to Kansas again.”
s.note: אֵיךְ חוֹזְרִים: a plural present-tense verb with no subject means "one, people in general". It is the usual way to ask for directions or instructions: אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לַתַּחֲנָה? (how do you get to the station?). The future נֵלֵךְ often works as "let's go".

s.line: She closed the door, locked it, and put the key carefully in the pocket of her dress.
s.note: נָעַל = to lock, and also to put on shoes; נַעַל is a shoe. So נָעֲלָה אֶת הַדֶּלֶת = she locked the door, while נָעֲלָה נַעֲלַיִם = she put on shoes. נָעוּל = locked. מַפְתֵּחַ (key) is from פָּתַח (to open).

w: יָצְאָה לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: And so, with Toto trotting along soberly behind her, she started on her journey.
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out, start a journey, also figuratively: הַפְּרוֹיֶקְט יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ (the project got under way). כְּשֶׁ + a present participle = "with X doing …": כְּשֶׁטּוֹטוֹ צוֹעֵד אַחֲרֶיהָ.

s.line: There were several roads nearby, but it did not take her long to find the one paved with yellow bricks.
s.note: לָקַח לָהּ זְמַן = it took her (a long) time; the person comes with לְ: כַּמָּה זְמַן זֶה יִקַּח לְךָ? (how long will it take you?). עָשׂוּי = made (of), a pa'ul participle of עָשָׂה: עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (made of wood). דֶּרֶךְ is normally feminine, hence הָעֲשׂוּיָה.

s.line: Within a short time she was walking briskly toward the Emerald City,
s.note: לְעֵבֶר = toward, a slightly literary word you'll meet in news reports: הַמִּשְׁטָרָה יָרְתָה לְעֵבֶר הָרֶכֶב. In speech people say לְכִוּוּן. מֶרֶץ = energy, vigor; נִמְרָץ = energetic.

s.line: her silver shoes tinkling merrily on the hard, yellow road-bed.
s.note: צִלְצֵל = to ring, jingle, and in everyday speech "to phone": אֲנִי אֲצַלְצֵל אֵלֶיךָ מָחָר (I'll call you tomorrow). The noun צִלְצוּל is a ring or ringtone.

s.line: The sun shone bright and the birds sang sweetly,
s.note: Hebrew often makes adverbs from בְּ + an abstract noun: בְּבָהִירוּת (with brightness), בִּמְתִיקוּת (with sweetness), בִּזְהִירוּת (carefully), בִּרְצִינוּת (seriously). שֶׁמֶשׁ is usually feminine.

w: שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר הָיָה|one might|~lit. that it was possible
שֶׁנֶּחְטְפָה|who had been whisked away|!nif'al · ח־ט־ף
s.line: and Dorothy did not feel nearly so bad as you might think a little girl would who had been suddenly whisked away from her own country and set down in the midst of a strange land.
s.note: Two passives here. נֶחְטְפָה is the nif'al of חָטַף (to snatch, grab, kidnap): "was snatched". הוּנְחָה is the hof'al of הֵנִיחַ (to put down): "was put down", the same root as מֻנָּח in sentence 21. זָר = foreign, strange; אֶרֶץ זָרָה = a foreign land, זָרִים = strangers.

s.line: She was surprised, as she walked along, to see how pretty the country was about her.
s.note: הֻפְתַּע is hof'al, the passive of hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise): הִיא הִפְתִּיעָה אוֹתוֹ → הוּא הֻפְתַּע. The noun is הַפְתָּעָה, a surprise, as in מְסִבַּת הַפְתָּעָה. נוֹף = landscape, view.

s.line: There were neat fences at the sides of the road, painted a dainty blue color,
s.note: מְסֻדָּר (pu'al participle of סִדֵּר, to arrange) = "arranged", hence neat, tidy: הַחֶדֶר מְסֻדָּר. צָבוּעַ = painted, a pa'ul participle of צָבַע (to paint, color), the same root as צֶבַע (color, paint).

s.line: and beyond them were fields of grain and vegetables in abundance.
s.note: הִשְׂתָּרֵעַ = to stretch out, extend (over an area). In hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first root letter שׂ/שׁ/ס: not *הִתְשָׂרֵעַ but הִשְׂתָּרֵעַ, just as הִסְתַּכֵּל. בְּשֶׁפַע = in plenty; שׁוֹפֵעַ = abundant.

s.line: Evidently the Munchkins were good farmers and able to raise large crops.
s.note: כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, evidently, literally "as is seen", from the nif'al נִרְאֶה. יָדַע + infinitive = to know how to: הוּא יוֹדֵעַ לְבַשֵּׁל (he can cook). גִּדֵּל (pi'el) = to grow crops, raise animals or children; גָּדַל (pa'al) = to grow up.

s.line: Once in a while she would pass a house, and the people came out to look at her and bow low as she went by;
s.note: מִדֵּי פַּעַם = from time to time, now and then, very common. קָדוּ קִידָה is the verb + noun pattern you know. A deep bow is עֲמֻקָּה (deep), not "low".

s.line: for everyone knew she had been the means of destroying the Wicked Witch and setting them free from bondage.
s.note: בִּזְכוּת = thanks to (something good); the opposite is בִּגְלַל (because of), often for something bad. הֻשְׁמַד (hof'al of הִשְׁמִיד, to destroy) and שֻׁחְרַר (pu'al of שִׁחְרֵר, to release) are both passives. שִׁחְרוּר is also discharge from the army: הוּא הִשְׁתַּחְרֵר מֵהַצָּבָא.

s.line: The houses of the Munchkins were odd-looking dwellings, for each was round, with a big dome for a roof.
s.note: מְשֻׁנֶּה = strange, odd; in form a pu'al participle of שִׁנָּה (to change), so literally "altered". כִּפָּה = a dome, and also a kippah (skullcap), which has the same shape. בִּמְקוֹם = instead of, literally "in the place of".

s.line: All were painted blue, for in this country of the East blue was the favorite color.
s.note: אָהוּב = loved, beloved, a pa'ul participle of אָהַב; הַצֶּבַע הָאָהוּב עָלַי = my favorite color (note עַל: אָהוּב עַל).

s.line: Toward evening, when Dorothy was tired with her long walk and began to wonder where she should pass the night,
s.note: תָּהָה = to wonder, ponder (somewhat literary); in speech you'd hear שָׁאֲלָה אֶת עַצְמָהּ. הֶעֱבִיר (hif'il of עָבַר, to pass) = to make pass, so "to spend" time: אֵיךְ הֶעֱבַרְתֶּם אֶת הַחֻפְשָׁה? (how did you spend the vacation?). It also means "to transfer, move": לְהַעֲבִיר כֶּסֶף.

s.line: she came to a house rather larger than the rest.
s.note: Comparison: יוֹתֵר + adjective + מִ: יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל מֵהַשְּׁאָר = bigger than the rest. הַשְּׁאָר = the rest, from the same root as נִשְׁאַר (to remain) in sentence 1.

s.line: On the green lawn before it many men and women were dancing.
s.note: דֶּשֶׁא = grass, lawn; signs say אָסוּר לִדְרֹךְ עַל הַדֶּשֶׁא (keep off the grass). With a mixed group the adjective is masculine plural: גְּבָרִים וְנָשִׁים רַבִּים.

w: הֲכִי חָזָק שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר|as loudly as possible|~idiom: the most strongly possible
s.line: Five little fiddlers played as loudly as possible,
s.note: נִגֵּן (pi'el) = to play an instrument; שִׂחֵק is to play a game. מְנַגֵּן = a player, and נִגּוּן is a tune, especially a Hasidic melody. הֲכִי … שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר = as … as possible: הֲכִי מַהֵר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר (as fast as possible). כַּנָּר = violinist, from כִּנּוֹר (violin).

s.line: and the people were laughing and singing,

w: בְּקִרְבַת מָקוֹם|near by|~idiom: in the nearness of place
s.line: while a big table near by was loaded with delicious fruits and nuts, pies and cakes, and many other good things to eat.
s.note: עָמוּס = loaded, a pa'ul participle of עָמַס (to load). You'll hear it every day for traffic and schedules: הַכְּבִישׁ עָמוּס (the road is jammed), יֵשׁ לִי יוֹם עָמוּס (I have a busy day). בְּקִרְבַת מָקוֹם = nearby, a fixed phrase common in news reports.

s.line: The people greeted Dorothy kindly, and invited her to supper and to pass the night with them;
s.note: אֵצֶל = at someone's place, like French "chez": אֲנִי אֵצֶל סַבְתָּא (I'm at Grandma's), לִישֹׁן אֵצֶל חָבֵר (to sleep over at a friend's). הִזְמִין = to invite, and also to order: לְהַזְמִין פִּיצָה, הַזְמָנָה (an invitation, a reservation, an order).

w: הָעֲשִׁירִים בְּיוֹתֵר|the richest|~lit. the rich in most
s.line: for this was the home of one of the richest Munchkins in the land,
s.note: The superlative: adjective + בְּיוֹתֵר (written style) or הֲכִי + adjective (speech): הֶעָשִׁיר בְּיוֹתֵר = הֲכִי עָשִׁיר. אֶחָד הַ… = "one of the …", with no מִ needed.

s.line: and his friends were gathered with him to celebrate their freedom from the bondage of the Wicked Witch.
s.note: הִתְאַסֵּף (hitpa'el) = to gather, assemble (of people); אָסַף (pa'al) = to collect something. לַחְגֹּג = to celebrate, from the same root as חַג (a holiday). שִׁעְבּוּד = subjugation, enslavement; it is also the legal word for a lien or mortgage on property.

s.line: Dorothy ate a hearty supper and was waited upon by the rich Munchkin himself,
s.note: הִגִּישׁ (hif'il) = to serve food, and also to submit: לְהַגִּישׁ עֲבוֹדָה (to hand in an assignment). A waiter is מֶלְצַר. מַשְׂבִּיעַ = filling, "making full", from שָׂבֵעַ (full, sated): אֲנִי שָׂבֵעַ = I'm full. Hebrew prefers the active here, where English has "was waited upon by".

s.line: whose name was Boq.
Then she sat upon a settee and watched the people dance.
s.note: הִתְבּוֹנֵן בְּ = to watch closely, observe, from the root of הֵבִין (to understand). It takes בְּ, like הִסְתַּכֵּל בְּ and הִבִּיט בְּ.

s.line: When Boq saw her silver shoes he said,
“You must be a great sorceress.”
s.note: בֶּטַח here expresses a confident guess: "you must be". קוֹסֶמֶת is the feminine of קוֹסֵם (wizard, magician), the word used for the Wizard of Oz himself. At a children's party the קוֹסֵם is the magician doing tricks.

s.line: “Why?” asked the girl.
“Because you wear silver shoes and have killed the Wicked Witch.
s.note: נוֹעֶלֶת: shoes are "worn" with נָעַל, the verb from sentence 29; clothes are worn with לָבַשׁ, and a hat or glasses with חָבַשׁ or הִרְכִּיב. הָרַגְתְּ ends in תְּ for "you" (feminine).

s.line: Besides, you have white in your frock, and only witches and sorceresses wear white.”
s.note: חוּץ מִזֶּה = besides, in addition, very common in speech; חוּץ מִ alone = except. שֶׁלָּךְ is the feminine "your".

s.line: “My dress is blue and white checked,” said Dorothy, smoothing out the wrinkles in it.
s.note: יִשֵּׁר (pi'el) = to straighten, smooth out, from יָשָׁר (straight). Pi'el often means "to make something X": יָשָׁר → יִשֵּׁר. קֶמֶט = a wrinkle or crease; מְקֻמָּט = wrinkled.

s.line: “It is kind of you to wear that,” said Boq.
s.note: נֶחְמָד מִצִּדְּךָ (to a woman מִצִּדֵּךְ) = "nice of you", literally "from your side". You'll hear תּוֹדָה, זֶה מְאֹד נֶחְמָד מִצִּדְּךָ constantly. מִצִּדִּי also means "as far as I'm concerned": מִצִּדִּי, תַּעֲשֶׂה מָה שֶׁאַתָּה רוֹצֶה.

s.line: “Blue is the color of the Munchkins, and white is the witch color.
s.note: הוּא between subject and predicate works as "is" (a copula): כָּחֹל הוּא הַצֶּבַע. It is optional, but common when both sides are nouns.

s.line: So we know you are a friendly witch.”
s.note: יְדִידוּתִי = friendly, from יָדִיד (friend). It's common in modern usage: יְדִידוּתִי לַסְּבִיבָה (environmentally friendly), יְדִידוּתִי לַמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ (user-friendly).

s.line: Dorothy did not know what to say to this,
for all the people seemed to think her a witch,
s.note: נִרְאָה שֶׁ = "it seems/seemed that", the impersonal use of נִרְאֶה. The present tense חוֹשְׁבִים inside a past-tense story is normal in Hebrew reported thought.

s.line: and she knew very well she was only an ordinary little girl who had come by the chance of a cyclone into a strange land.
s.note: רָגִיל = ordinary, usual; כָּרָגִיל = as usual, and הִתְרַגֵּל לְ = to get used to. The Hebrew turns "who had come by the chance of a cyclone" around: "whom the tornado brought by chance".

w: כְּשֶׁנִּמְאַס לָהּ|when she had tired|~idiom: when it became loathsome to her
s.line: When she had tired watching the dancing, Boq led her into the house, where he gave her a room with a pretty bed in it.
s.note: נִמְאַס לִי = I'm fed up, I've had enough, one of the most common phrases in spoken Hebrew. The person who is fed up comes with לְ, and the thing comes as subject or infinitive: נִמְאַס לִי מֵהַגֶּשֶׁם, נִמְאַס לָהּ לְחַכּוֹת. הוֹבִיל (to lead) appeared in chapter 1 meaning "to haul".

s.line: The sheets were made of blue cloth,
and Dorothy slept soundly in them till morning, with Toto curled up on the blue rug beside her.
s.note: מְכֻרְבָּל = curled up, snugly wrapped; the active-reflexive form is הִתְכַּרְבֵּל: הִתְכַּרְבַּלְתִּי בַּשְּׂמִיכָה (I snuggled up in the blanket). שָׁכַב = to be lying (the state), as opposed to נִשְׁכַּב (to lie down).

s.line: She ate a hearty breakfast,
and watched a wee Munchkin baby, who played with Toto and pulled his tail and crowed and laughed in a way that greatly amused Dorothy.
s.note: קְטַנְטַן = tiny, a diminutive made by repeating the last syllable of קָטָן; likewise כֶּלֶב → כְּלַבְלַב (puppy). מָשַׁךְ לוֹ בַּזָּנָב: you pull on something with בְּ, and the לוֹ marks whose tail it is, a very common pattern with body parts: הִיא נָגְעָה לוֹ בַּיָּד. שִׁעְשֵׁעַ = to amuse; שַׁעֲשׁוּעַ = amusement, fun.

s.line: Toto was a fine curiosity to all the people, for they had never seen a dog before.
s.note: עוֹרֵר = to arouse, stir up (interest, curiosity, debate); it is the pi'el form of a hollow root, also seen in שָׁעוֹן מְעוֹרֵר (alarm clock). Here Hebrew says the dog "aroused curiosity" rather than "was a curiosity". סַקְרָן = curious; סַקְרָנוּת = curiosity.

s.line: “How far is it to the Emerald City?” the girl asked.
s.note: כַּמָּה רָחוֹק = how far. Hebrew needs no "it is" here: כַּמָּה רָחוֹק מִכָּאן לְ…? is the standard way to ask a distance.

s.line: “I do not know,” answered Boq gravely, “for I have never been there.

w: יֵשׁ לָהֶם|they have|~lit. there is to them
s.line: It is better for people to keep away from Oz, unless they have business with him.
s.note: עָדִיף = preferable, "it's better": עָדִיף לְחַכּוֹת (better to wait); עָדִיף לִי = I'd rather. אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן = unless, a fixed three-word phrase. הִתְרַחֵק מִ (hitpa'el) = to move away from, from רָחוֹק (far).

s.line: But it is a long way to the Emerald City, and it will take you many days.
s.note: תִּקַּח is the future of לָקַח: the ל drops out and the ק is doubled, just like יִקַּח. This is the same "take time" idiom as לָקַח לָהּ זְמַן in sentence 31.

s.line: The country here is rich and pleasant, but you must pass through rough and dangerous places before you reach the end of your journey.”
s.note: הִצְטָרֵךְ = to need to, have to (hitpa'el of צָרִיךְ). Its ת swaps with the צ and turns into ט: הִצְטָרֵךְ, not *הִתְצָרֵךְ. אֶרֶץ is feminine: עֲשִׁירָה וּנְעִימָה. מְסֻכָּן = dangerous, a pu'al participle in form ("endangered"); סַכָּנָה = danger.

s.line: This worried Dorothy a little,
s.note: הִדְאִיג (hif'il) = to make someone worry; דָּאַג (pa'al) = to worry oneself, and also to take care of: אֲנִי אֶדְאַג לְזֶה (I'll take care of it). Hif'il often makes the "causing" version of a pa'al verb.

s.line: but she knew that only the Great Oz could help her get to Kansas again,
s.note: עָזַר לְ: in Hebrew you help to someone, so it is לַעֲזֹר לָהּ, never אוֹתָהּ. אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲזֹר לְךָ? = can I help you?

w: לַחֲזֹר עַל עִקְבוֹתֶיהָ|to turn back|~idiom: to return on her footsteps
s.line: so she bravely resolved not to turn back.
s.note: חָזַר עַל עִקְבוֹתָיו = to retrace one's steps, turn back, a set phrase with the possessive ending changing for the person: עִקְבוֹתַי, עִקְבוֹתֶיהָ. חָזַר עַל alone means "to repeat": תַּחֲזֹר עַל זֶה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.

w: בְּדֶרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|along the yellow brick road
s.line: She bade her friends good-bye, and again started along the road of yellow brick.
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ = to part from, say goodbye to. It is nif'al with an active meaning, and it takes מִ: נִפְרַדְנוּ מֵהֶם בַּשְּׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה. Of a couple, הֵם נִפְרְדוּ = they broke up. הִמְשִׁיךְ = to continue; הֶמְשֵׁךְ = continuation, sequel.

w: שֶׁכְּדַאי|that it would be good|~idiom: worthwhile
s.line: When she had gone several miles she thought she would stop to rest,
s.note: כְּדַאי = worthwhile, a good idea: כְּדַאי לְךָ לָבוֹא (you should come), לֹא כְּדַאי (better not). זֶה לֹא שָׁוֶה is its near-synonym for "not worth it". לָנוּחַ = to rest, from the same root as נוֹחַ (comfortable) and מְנוּחָה (rest).

s.line: and so climbed to the top of the fence beside the road and sat down.
s.note: הִתְיַשֵּׁב (hitpa'el) = to sit down, the action; יָשַׁב = to sit, be sitting. תִּתְיַשֵּׁב! = have a seat! טִפֵּס = to climb; טִפּוּס is climbing as a sport.

s.line: There was a great cornfield beyond the fence,
and not far away she saw a Scarecrow, placed high on a pole to keep the birds from the ripe corn.
s.note: הֻצַּב is hof'al, the passive of הִצִּיב (to set up, station): "was set up". You'll read it in the news about soldiers or equipment: חַיָּלִים הֻצְּבוּ בַּגְּבוּל. הִרְחִיק (hif'il) = to keep away, to make far; compare הִתְרַחֵק (to move away oneself) in sentence 76.

s.line: Dorothy leaned her chin upon her hand and gazed thoughtfully at the Scarecrow.
s.note: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחְשָׁבוֹת = lost in thought, literally "sunk in thoughts"; שָׁקַע = to sink, and the sun שׁוֹקַעַת (sets). הִשְׁעִין (hif'il) = to lean something; נִשְׁעַן (nif'al) = to lean oneself, and a מִשְׁעָנָה is the back of a chair. Body parts usually take הַ, not a possessive: הַסַּנְטֵר, הַיָּד.

s.line: Its head was a small sack stuffed with straw,
s.note: מְמֻלָּא is the pu'al participle of מִלֵּא (to fill), from sentence 4: "filled", here "stuffed". In the kitchen מְמֻלָּאִים are stuffed vegetables, a favorite Israeli dish. The Scarecrow is masculine in Hebrew, so שֶׁלּוֹ, although Baum switches between "its" and "his".

s.line: with eyes, nose, and mouth painted on it to represent a face.
s.note: מְצֻיָּר = drawn or painted (a picture), pu'al participle of צִיֵּר (to draw); צִיּוּר = a drawing, סֶרֶט מְצֻיָּר = a cartoon. Contrast צָבוּעַ (painted a color) in sentence 37. פָּנִים (face) is always plural in form.

s.line: An old, pointed blue hat, that had belonged to some Munchkin, was perched on his head,
s.note: מְחֻדָּד = pointed, sharpened (pu'al of חִדֵּד, to sharpen), from חַד (sharp). אֵיזֶשֶׁהוּ = some (or other), masculine; feminine אֵיזוֹשֶׁהִי: אֵיזֶשֶׁהוּ בָּחוּר, אֵיזוֹשֶׁהִי בְּעָיָה.

s.line: and the rest of the figure was a blue suit of clothes, worn and faded, which had also been stuffed with straw.
s.note: מֻלְּאָה is a finite pu'al verb, "was filled", the past-tense partner of מְמֻלָּא: pi'el מִלֵּא (filled) → pu'al מֻלָּא (was filled). חֲלִיפָה = a suit, and also an exchange; הֶחֱלִיף = to change, swap.

s.line: On the feet were some old boots with blue tops, such as every man wore in this country,
and the figure was raised above the stalks of corn by means of the pole stuck up its back.
s.note: הֻרַם (hof'al) = was raised, the passive of הֵרִים (to lift) from sentence 26. תָּקוּעַ = stuck in, a pa'ul participle of תָּקַע (to thrust, stick in). In everyday speech: אֲנִי תָּקוּעַ בַּפְּקָק (I'm stuck in traffic), הַמַּחְשֵׁב תָּקוּעַ (the computer is frozen). בְּעֶזְרַת = with the help of, by means of.

s.line: While Dorothy was looking earnestly into the queer, painted face of the Scarecrow,
s.note: פָּנִים is plural in form, so its adjectives are plural: הַפָּנִים הַמּוּזָרִים. בְּרִכּוּז = with concentration; הִתְרַכֵּז = to concentrate, and a מֶרְכָּז is a center.

s.line: she was surprised to see one of the eyes slowly wink at her.
s.note: קָרַץ לְ = to wink at; קְרִיצָה = a wink. Figuratively, something that קוֹרֵץ לִי appeals to me, tempts me: הָרַעְיוֹן הַזֶּה מְאֹד קוֹרֵץ לִי. עַיִן is feminine, hence אַחַת and קוֹרֶצֶת.

s.line: She thought she must have been mistaken at first, for none of the scarecrows in Kansas ever wink;
s.note: טָעָה = to make a mistake, be wrong; טָעוּת = a mistake, and בְּטָעוּת = by mistake. אֲנִי טוֹעֶה? = am I wrong? This sentence stacks the double negative you know: אַף אֶחָד … לֹא … אַף פַּעַם.

s.line: but presently the figure nodded its head to her in a friendly way.
s.note: הִנְהֵן = to nod (in agreement); present מְהַנְהֵן. בְּאֹפֶן + adjective is a regular way to make an adverb: בְּאֹפֶן יְדִידוּתִי (in a friendly way), בְּאֹפֶן אִישִׁי (personally). דְּמוּת (figure, character) is feminine, so הִנְהֲנָה and בְּרֹאשָׁהּ.

s.line: Then she climbed down from the fence and walked up to it, while Toto ran around the pole and barked.
s.note: נִגַּשׁ אֶל = to approach, go up to (nif'al, active meaning). It shares its root with הִגִּישׁ (to serve, to bring near) earlier in this chapter. נִגַּשׁ לְמִבְחָן = to sit an exam.

s.line: “Good day,” said the Scarecrow, in a rather husky voice.
s.note: צָרוּד = hoarse; אֲנִי צָרוּד is what you say when you've lost your voice. דֵּי = rather, quite (דֵּי טוֹב), and alone דַּי! means "enough!". Israelis greet with שָׁלוֹם or בֹּקֶר טוֹב; יוֹם טוֹב today mostly means "have a good day" or a festival.

s.line: “Did you speak?” asked the girl, in wonder.
s.note: A yes/no question in speech is just a statement with rising intonation: דִּבַּרְתָּ?. פְּלִיאָה = wonder, amazement; נִפְלָא = wonderful.

s.line: “Certainly,” answered the Scarecrow.

w: מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ|how do you do|~lit. what is your peace (fem.)
s.line: “How do you do?”
s.note: מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? (to a man) / מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ? (to a woman) = how are you?, literally "what is your peace?". Casually: מָה נִשְׁמַע? or מָה קוֹרֶה?.

s.line: “I’m pretty well, thank you,” replied Dorothy politely.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שָׁב, to return) = to reply, a more literary word than עָנָה; תְּשׁוּבָה = an answer. נִימוּס = politeness; מְנֻמָּס = polite.

w: מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ|how do you do|~lit. what is your peace (masc.)
s.line: “How do you do?”

w: יוֹם וָלַיְלָה|night and day|~idiom: day and night
s.line: “I’m not feeling well,” said the Scarecrow, with a smile, “for it is very tedious being perched up here night and day to scare away crows.”
s.note: מְשַׁעֲמֵם (active participle) = boring, while מְשֻׁעְמָם (pu'al, passive) = bored. A classic learner mistake: אֲנִי מְשַׁעֲמֵם means "I am boring"! הִבְרִיחַ (hif'il of בָּרַח, to flee) = to make flee, chase off; in the news it also means "to smuggle": הַבְרָחַת סַמִּים.

s.line: “Can’t you get down?” asked Dorothy.
“No, for this pole is stuck up my back.
If you will please take away the pole I shall be greatly obliged to you.”
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה = deeply grateful, literally "a prisoner of thanks", a fixed, rather formal phrase (fem. אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה). Everyday Hebrew says אֲנִי מַמָּשׁ מוֹדֶה לָךְ. הוֹצִיא (hif'il of יָצָא, to go out) = to take out; it also means to spend money: הוֹצֵאתִי הַרְבֵּה כֶּסֶף.

s.line: Dorothy reached up both arms and lifted the figure off the pole,
s.note: הוֹשִׁיט = to stretch out, hold out (a hand, an arm); הוֹשִׁיט יַד עֶזְרָה = to lend a helping hand. יָד is feminine, so "two hands" is שְׁתֵּי יָדַיִם; it covers both hand and arm.

s.line: for, being stuffed with straw, it was quite light.
“Thank you very much,” said the Scarecrow, when he had been set down on the ground.
s.note: הוּנַח (hof'al) = was put down, the masculine of הוּנְחָה that described Dorothy's arrival in Oz, and the source of מֻנָּח (lying). The whole family: הֵנִיחַ put down → הוּנַח was put down → מֻנָּח placed, lying.

w: בֶּן אָדָם|a man|~lit. son of Adam
s.line: “I feel like a new man.”
s.note: אֲנִי מַרְגִּישׁ כְּמוֹ בֶּן אָדָם חָדָשׁ is an everyday phrase in Hebrew too, said after a shower or a good night's sleep. בֶּן אָדָם = a person, a human being, and in speech often just "man!" or "dude".

s.line: Dorothy was puzzled at this,
s.note: מְבֻלְבָּל = confused, puzzled (pu'al participle of בִּלְבֵּל, to confuse, mix up). אַל תְּבַלְבֵּל אוֹתִי! = don't confuse me! בִּלְבּוּל = confusion, a mix-up.

s.line: for it sounded queer to hear a stuffed man speak, and to see him bow and walk along beside her.
s.note: After verbs of perception Hebrew uses a present participle for the action seen or heard: <t>לִשְׁמֹעַ אִישׁ מְדַבֵּר</t> = to hear a man speak(ing), <t>לִרְאוֹת אוֹתוֹ הוֹלֵךְ</t> = to see him walk(ing).

s.line: “Who are you?” asked the Scarecrow when he had stretched himself and yawned.
s.note: הִתְמַתַּח (hitpa'el) = to stretch oneself, the reflexive of מָתַח (to stretch something, pull tight). מֶתַח = tension, suspense, and a סֶרֶט מֶתַח is a thriller. פִּהֵק = to yawn; פִּהוּק = a yawn.

s.line: “And where are you going?”
s.note: לְאָן = where to, for motion, while אֵיפֹה = where, for location. לְאָן אַתָּה נוֹסֵעַ? but אֵיפֹה אַתָּה גָּר?.

w: קוֹרְאִים לִי|my name is|~idiom: (they) call me
s.line: “My name is Dorothy,” said the girl, “and I am going to the Emerald City, to ask the Great Oz to send me back to Kansas.”
s.note: קוֹרְאִים לִי ("they call to me") is the everyday way to give your name; אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ? = what's your name? בִּקֵּשׁ מִ: you ask from someone, and the request follows with שֶׁ + future: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא (I asked him to come). הֶחֱזִיר = to return something, give back.

s.line: “Where is the Emerald City?” he inquired.
s.note: נִמְצָא (nif'al of מָצָא, to find) = "is located", literally "is found". It is the normal way to say where something is: אֵיפֹה נִמְצֵאת הַתַּחֲנָה?. עִיר is feminine, hence נִמְצֵאת.

s.line: “And who is Oz?”
s.note: מִי זֶה = who is (that)?, the usual spoken form; זֶה acts like "is" here, as in מָה זֶה?.

s.line: “Why, don’t you know?” she returned, in surprise.
“No, indeed.
s.note: בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁלֹּא = "really not, no indeed", an emphatic no; the matching yes is בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁכֵּן. בֶּאֱמֶת? alone = really?

s.line: I don’t know anything.

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there is not to me
s.line: You see, I am stuffed, so I have no brains at all,” he answered sadly.
s.note: מֹחַ = brain; "brains" in the sense of intelligence is often שֵׂכֶל: אֵין לוֹ שֵׂכֶל = he has no sense. אַתְּ מְבִינָה / אַתָּה מֵבִין ("you understand") is the spoken filler for "you see".

s.line: “Oh,” said Dorothy, “I’m awfully sorry for you.”
s.note: נוֹרָא = terrible, but in speech it is also an intensifier, "awfully": נוֹרָא נֶחְמָד (awfully nice). מִצְטַעֵר = sorry (hitpa'el, with the ת turned to ט after צ, as in הִצְטָרֵךְ); אֲנִי מִצְטַעֶרֶת is also how a woman says "I'm sorry" as an apology.

s.line: “Do you think,” he asked, “if I go to the Emerald City with you, that Oz would give me some brains?”
s.note: After אִם (if), Hebrew uses the future for a future condition, where English uses the present: אִם אֵלֵךְ = "if I go". יִתֵּן is the future of נָתַן: the first נ drops out, leaving the doubled תּ.

s.line: “I cannot tell,” she returned, “but you may come with me, if you like.
s.note: יָכוֹל covers both "can" and "may": אַתָּה יָכוֹל לָבוֹא = you can / may come. Dorothy says יְכוֹלָה (feminine), the Scarecrow יָכוֹל. אִם אַתָּה רוֹצֶה = if you like, if you want.

s.line: If Oz will not give you any brains you will be no worse off than you are now.”
s.note: גָּרוּעַ = bad, poor in quality; גָּרוּעַ יוֹתֵר = worse. מַצָּב = situation, condition; מָה הַמַּצָּב? is a casual "how's it going?", and you'll hear הַמַּצָּב in the news for the security situation.

s.line: “That is true,” said the Scarecrow.
“You see,” he continued confidentially, “I don’t mind my legs and arms and body being stuffed, because I cannot get hurt.
s.note: לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי = I don't mind, I don't care, an essential everyday phrase. As a question, אִכְפַּת לְךָ אִם …? = do you mind if …? נִפְגַּע (nif'al) = to be hurt, injured, the passive of פָּגַע בְּ (to hit, hurt). In the news, נִפְגָּעִים are casualties.

w: זֶה לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה|it doesn't matter|~idiom: it doesn't change
s.line: If anyone treads on my toes or sticks a pin into me, it doesn’t matter, for I can’t feel it.
s.note: זֶה לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה = it doesn't matter, literally "it doesn't change (anything)", from pi'el שִׁנָּה. תּוֹקֵעַ is the active of תָּקוּעַ (stuck) from sentence 93. אֶצְבַּע covers both fingers and toes; to be precise, toes are אֶצְבְּעוֹת הָרַגְלַיִם.

s.line: But I do not want people to call me a fool,
s.note: רָצָה שֶׁ + future = to want someone else to do something: אֲנִי רוֹצֶה שֶׁתָּבוֹא (I want you to come). Hebrew can't say "want you to come" with an infinitive. קָרָא לְ X = to call someone X, the same idiom as קוֹרְאִים לִי.

s.line: and if my head stays stuffed with straw instead of with brains, as yours is, how am I ever to know anything?”
s.note: אֵי פַּעַם = ever (at any time), in questions and positive sentences; with a negative you use אַף פַּעַם. הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת? = have you ever been to Eilat? יִשָּׁאֵר is the future of נִשְׁאַר from sentence 1.

s.line: “I understand how you feel,” said the little girl, who was truly sorry for him.
s.note: רִחֵם עַל (pi'el) = to pity, feel sorry for, with עַל; רַחֲמִים = mercy, compassion. Compare מִצְטַעֵר (sorry, apologetic) in sentence 124.

s.line: “If you will come with me I’ll ask Oz to do all he can for you.”

w: בְּהַכָּרַת תּוֹדָה|gratefully|~lit. with recognition of thanks
s.line: “Thank you,” he answered gratefully.
s.note: הַכָּרַת תּוֹדָה = gratitude, literally "recognition of thanks"; הַכָּרָה is from הִכִּיר (to know, recognize). The same הַכָּרָה means consciousness: הוּא אִבֵּד אֶת הַהַכָּרָה (he lost consciousness).

s.line: They walked back to the road.

w: בְּדֶרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|along the yellow brick road
s.line: Dorothy helped him over the fence, and they started along the path of yellow brick for the Emerald City.
s.note: עָבַר אֶת = to get over, cross (a fence, a road, a test): עָבַרְתִּי אֶת הַמִּבְחָן (I passed the test). Again עָזְרָה לוֹ, help to him.

s.line: Toto did not like this addition to the party at first.
s.note: חֲבוּרָה = a group, band of companions, from חָבֵר (friend). A "party" in the sense of a celebration is מְסִבָּה, and a political party is מִפְלָגָה. תּוֹסֶפֶת = an addition, also a side dish or a pay supplement.

s.line: He smelled around the stuffed man as if he suspected there might be a nest of rats in the straw,
s.note: רִחְרֵחַ = to sniff around, a doubled root from רֵיחַ (smell); a nosy person מְרַחְרֵחַ too. חָשַׁד = to suspect; חָשׁוּד = a suspect, a word you hear in every crime report. עַכְבָּר = mouse, עַכְבְּרוֹשׁ = rat.

s.line: and he often growled in an unfriendly way at the Scarecrow.
s.note: נָהַם עַל = to growl at, with עַל like נָבַח עַל in sentence 5. לֹא יְדִידוּתִי: Hebrew often makes the opposite of an adjective with לֹא, as in לֹא נָעִים (unpleasant) and לֹא חֻקִּי (illegal).

s.line: “Don’t mind Toto,” said Dorothy to her new friend.
s.note: A negative command is <t>אַל</t> + future: <t>אַל תָּשִׂים לֵב</t> = don't pay attention, <t>אַל תִּדְאַג</t> = don't worry. This is the <t>שָׂם לֵב</t> from sentence 18.

s.line: “He never bites.”
“Oh, I’m not afraid,” replied the Scarecrow.
“He can’t hurt the straw.
s.note: הִזִּיק לְ = to harm, damage, with לְ; נֶזֶק = damage, and מַזִּיק = harmful: עִשּׁוּן מַזִּיק לַבְּרִיאוּת (smoking is harmful to health), the warning on every cigarette pack.

s.line: Do let me carry that basket for you.
s.note: תֵּן לִי / תְּנִי לִי (to a woman) = "give me", and also "let me": תְּנִי לִי לַעֲזֹר (let me help). לָשֵׂאת = to carry (a bit formal; in speech also לְהַחֲזִיק or לְסַחֵב). It also appears in לָשֵׂאת אִשָּׁה (to marry) and לָשֵׂאת נְאוּם (to give a speech).

s.line: I shall not mind it, for I can’t get tired.
s.note: הִפְרִיעַ לְ = to bother, disturb, interrupt: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה לְהַפְרִיעַ (I don't want to disturb), זֶה מַפְרִיעַ לְךָ? (does it bother you?). הִתְעַיֵּף (hitpa'el) = to get tired, from עָיֵף (tired).

w: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי|while|~idiom: in the course of
s.line: I’ll tell you a secret,” he continued, as he walked along.
s.note: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי + noun = while doing, in the course of: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי נְסִיעָה (while driving), תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי שִׂיחָה (in the middle of a conversation). סִפֵּר (pi'el) = to tell; it is the same root as סֵפֶר (book) and סִפּוּר (story).

s.line: “There is only one thing in the world I am afraid of.”
s.note: שֶׁאֲנִי פּוֹחֵד מִמֶּנּוּ: a Hebrew relative clause needs a pronoun pointing back to the noun, here מִמֶּנּוּ ("of it"), because פָּחַד takes מִ. English ends with a dangling "of"; Hebrew can't.

s.line: “What is that?” asked Dorothy;
“the Munchkin farmer who made you?”
“No,” answered the Scarecrow; “it’s a lighted match.”
s.note: דּוֹלֵק = burning, lit (pa'al); הִדְלִיק (hif'il) = to light, switch on: תַּדְלִיק אֶת הָאוֹר (turn on the light). From the same root: דֶּלֶק (fuel) and תַּחֲנַת דֶּלֶק (gas station). A straw man has good reason to fear one.
